questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Kinetic Energy of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(3{t}^{2}+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (3{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0={0}^{3}+0+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}+t.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)={1}^{3}+1=2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)={2}^{3}+2=10\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =150-6 \\  & =144\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(4t+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=4t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
3=2(0)^{2}+0+C\,⟹\,C=3.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{2}+t+3.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)^{2}+1+3=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)^{2}+2+3=13\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {13}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =338-72 \\  & =266\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $5t\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=2\,s$ and $t=4\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=5t,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(2)=5(2)=10\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(4)=5(4)=20\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1.5\cdot (20)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1.5\cdot (10)^{2} \\  & =300-75 \\  & =225\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $6\sqrt{x}\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}6\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =4(8-1) \\  & =28\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=4$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 28 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot (2\sqrt{2})^{2} \\ 28 & =\frac{1}{2}{v}_{1}^{2}-4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{1}^{2} & =32 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =64 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 8.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=4$ is $8\,m/s.$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle to Find a Particle's Velocity
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $3x\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=4,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =24-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{45}{2}\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{45}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{45}{2} & =\frac{125}{2}-\frac{5}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =40 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=5-4=1\,m/s.
$$
